summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity shows that 5 is a square modulo such a prime \(p\); choosing an even square root \(r\) and setting \(n=r-1\) gives an odd \(n\le p-2\) with \(p\mid n^2+2n-4\). Writing the continued fraction via continuants gives unreduced numerator \(F=n^2+2n-4\), and a factorial determinant identity shows that the cofactor \(F/p\) cancels from the denominator while \(p\) cannot (since \(n<p\)), so the reduced numerator—and hence the required denominator—is exactly \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}\qquad(2\le k<n-1),
\]
with final value
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac{n}{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is
\[
C_n=\frac1{R_2(n)}.
\]
If the reduced form of \(R_2(n)\) has numerator \(N\), then the reduced denominator of \(C_n\) is \(|N|\). We prove that for every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\), one can choose \(n\) so that the reduced numerator of \(R_2(n)\) is exactly \(p\).

We first develop the needed formula for \(R_2(n)\).

Define integers \(b_j\) by
\[
b_0=0,\qquad b_1=1,
\]
and, for \(k\ge0\),
\[
b_{k+2}=(k+3)(b_{k+1}-b_k).
\]
These are continuants associated with the initial part of the continued fraction. They satisfy the determinant identity
\[
2\bigl((k+1)b_{k+1}-(k+2)b_k\bigr)=(k+2)!.
\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for \(k=0\), the left side is \(2(1\cdot1-2\cdot0)=2=2!\). If (1) holds for \(k\), then the left side at \(k+1\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl((k+2)b_{k+2}-(k+3)b_{k+1}\bigr)
&=2(k+3)\bigl((k+2)(b_{k+1}-b_k)-b_{k+1}\bigr)\\
&=(k+3)\,2\bigl((k+1)b_{k+1}-(k+2)b_k\bigr)\\
&=(k+3)(k+2)!=(k+3)!,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves the identity by induction.

We will also need to know that all the rational quantities occurring in the continued fraction are positive, so in particular no recursive division is by zero. More precisely, for \(n\ge3\) and \(2\le k\le n-1\),
\[
R_k(n)>0
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
k(k-2)<(k-1)R_k(n).
\tag{2}
\]
This is proved by backward induction on \(k\). At \(k=n-1\), write \(k=n-1\). Then
\[
R_k(n)=k+\frac n4>0,
\]
and
\[
(k-1)R_k(n)-k(k-2)
=k+\frac{(k-1)n}{4}>0.
\]
Now suppose (2) holds at \(k+1\), and put \(T=R_{k+1}(n)>0\). The second inequality at \(k+1\) says
\[
(k+1)(k-1)<kT.
\tag{3}
\]
Since \(k\ge2\), (3) also implies \(kT>k+1\), and hence
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{T}>0.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T\bigl((k-1)R_k(n)-k(k-2)\bigr)
&=T\left((k-1)\left(k-\frac{k+1}{T}\right)-k(k-2)\right)\\
&=kT-(k-1)(k+1)>0
\end{aligned}
\]
by (3). Since \(T>0\), the desired second inequality follows. This proves (2).

The prefix continuants give the following identity. Whenever \(m+3\le n-1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_2(n)\bigl(b_{m+1}R_{m+3}(n)-(m+3)b_m\bigr)
={}&(m+2)R_{m+3}(n)\\
&-(m+3)(m+1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]
For \(m=0\), this says
\[
R_2(n)R_3(n)=2R_3(n)-3,
\]
which is just the defining relation \(R_2(n)=2-3/R_3(n)\), multiplied by the nonzero number \(R_3(n)\). For the induction step, substitute
\[
R_{m+3}(n)=(m+3)-\frac{m+4}{R_{m+4}(n)}
\]
into (4), multiply through by the positive, hence nonzero, quantity \(R_{m+4}(n)\), and collect terms. Using
\[
b_{m+2}=(m+3)(b_{m+1}-b_m),
\]
the resulting identity is exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_2(n)\bigl(b_{m+2}R_{m+4}(n)-(m+4)b_{m+1}\bigr)
={}&(m+3)R_{m+4}(n)\\
&-(m+4)(m+2),
\end{aligned}
\]
which is (4) with \(m\) replaced by \(m+1\). Thus (4) follows by induction.

For \(m\ge0\), set
\[
D_m=4b_{m+1}+(m+3)b_m
\tag{5}
\]
and
\[
F_m=(m+3)^2+2(m+3)-4.
\tag{6}
\]
Then
\[
R_2(m+3)D_m=F_m.
\tag{7}
\]
For \(m=0\), this follows directly: \(R_2(3)=2+3/4=11/4\), \(D_0=4\), and \(F_0=11\). For \(m\ge1\), apply (4) with the prefix parameter \(m-1\) and with \(n=m+3\). Its tail is
\[
R_{m+2}(m+3)=(m+2)+\frac{m+3}{4}.
\]
After inserting this value and multiplying the identity by \(4\), the coefficient multiplying \(R_2(m+3)\) is
\[
4b_m\left((m+2)+\frac{m+3}{4}\right)-4(m+2)b_{m-1}.
\]
Since
\[
b_{m+1}=(m+2)(b_m-b_{m-1}),
\]
this coefficient is
\[
4b_{m+1}+(m+3)b_m=D_m.
\]
The right side becomes
\[
4(m+1)\left((m+2)+\frac{m+3}{4}\right)-4m(m+2)
=m^2+8m+11,
\]
and this is precisely
\[
(m+3)^2+2(m+3)-4=F_m.
\]
This proves (7).

A second crucial identity is
\[
2(m+2)D_m-2b_{m+1}F_m=-(m+3)!.
\tag{8}
\]
To obtain it, substitute the definitions (5) and (6) into the left side and collect the coefficients of \(b_{m+1}\) and \(b_m\). The result reduces exactly to \(-(m+3)\) times
\[
2\bigl((m+1)b_{m+1}-(m+2)b_m\bigr),
\]
which by (1) is \(-(m+3)(m+2)!)=-(m+3)!\). This proves (8).

We now construct an appropriate index from the congruence condition on \(p\). Let \(p\) be prime and suppose
\[
p\equiv1\quad\hbox{or}\quad9\pmod {10}.
\]
Then \(p\ge11\), \(p\) is odd, and
\[
p\equiv1\quad\hbox{or}\quad4\pmod5.
\]
Both \(1\) and \(4\) are nonzero squares modulo \(5\). Because \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), quadratic reciprocity gives
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right)=1.
\]
Consequently, there is a residue \(x\) modulo \(p\) such that
\[
x^2\equiv5\pmod p.
\tag{9}
\]
Choose its representative with \(0\le x<p\). This representative is nonzero, since otherwise \(p\mid5\), impossible for the primes under consideration. We may choose an even representative of a square root of \(5\): if \(x\) is even, put \(r=x\); if \(x\) is odd, put \(r=p-x\). Since \(p\) is odd, \(p-x\) is even in the second case, and
\[
(p-x)^2\equiv x^2\equiv5\pmod p.
\]
Thus in either case
\[
0<r<p,\qquad r\ \hbox{is even},\qquad r^2\equiv5\pmod p.
\tag{10}
\]
In fact \(r\ge4\). Since \(r\) is positive and even, the only contrary possibility is \(r=2\); but then (10) would imply \(4\equiv5\pmod p\), so \(p\mid1\), an impossibility.

Set
\[
n=r-1.
\]
Then \(n\ge3\), \(n\) is odd, and since \(r<p\),
\[
n+2=r+1\le p.
\tag{11}
\]
Moreover,
\[
n^2+2n-4=(r-1)^2+2(r-1)-4=r^2-5,
\]
so (10) gives
\[
p\mid n^2+2n-4.
\tag{12}
\]
Write \(n=m+3\), where \(m\ge0\). Then (11) becomes
\[
m+5\le p,
\tag{13}
\]
and (12) says \(p\mid F_m\). Since \(F_m>0\), write
\[
F_m=pc
\tag{14}
\]
with a positive integer \(c\).

The bound (13) gives an important estimate on this cofactor. Since \(p\ge n+2\),
\[
F_m=n^2+2n-4<n(n+2)\le np.
\]
Combining this with (14) yields
\[
0<c<n=m+3.
\tag{15}
\]
In particular, \(c\mid n!=(m+3)!\), because every positive integer at most \(n\) occurs as one of the factors of \(n!\).

We next show that \(c\) is coprime to \(2(m+2)=2(n-1)\). Since \(n\) is odd, write
\[
n=2t+1.
\]
A direct computation gives
\[
F_m=n^2+2n-4=4t^2+8t-1,
\]
whereas
\[
2(t+2)(n-1)=2(t+2)(2t)=4t^2+8t.
\]
Using \(F_m=pc\), we therefore have the explicit Bézout identity
\[
-pc+(t+2)\,2(n-1)=1.
\tag{16}
\]
Thus
\[
\gcd(c,2(n-1))=1.
\tag{17}
\]

We can now determine what cancels from (7). Since \(c\mid F_m\) and \(c\mid(m+3)!\), identity (8) shows that
\[
c\mid 2(m+2)D_m.
\]
By (17), \(c\) is coprime to \(2(m+2)\), so Euclid's lemma gives
\[
c\mid D_m.
\]
Write
\[
D_m=cd
\tag{18}
\]
for an integer \(d\). In fact \(d>0\). We know from (2) that \(R_2(m+3)>0\), while \(F_m>0\); hence (7) implies \(D_m>0\), and then (18), together with \(c>0\), gives \(d>0\).

It remains to prove that \(p\) does not also cancel from \(d\). Suppose for contradiction that \(p\mid d\). By (18), this would imply \(p\mid D_m\), while (14) gives \(p\mid F_m\). Identity (8) would then imply
\[
p\mid(m+3)!=n!.
\]
A prime dividing \(n!\) must divide one of the factors \(1,2,\ldots,n\), and therefore must be at most \(n\). This contradicts (13), which says \(p\ge n+2\). Hence
\[
\gcd(p,d)=1.
\tag{19}
\]

Finally, substitute (14) and (18) into (7). Since \(c\ne0\), cancellation gives
\[
R_2(m+3)=\frac{F_m}{D_m}=\frac{pc}{cd}=\frac pd.
\]
By (19) and \(d>0\), this is already in reduced form and has numerator \(p\). Therefore the reciprocal continued fraction \(C_{m+3}=1/R_2(m+3)\) has reduced denominator \(p\). In the notation of the sequence,
\[
a(m+3)=p.
\]
Thus every prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs in A363347, as claimed.
